items.title: Patients may miss out on NHS weight-loss jabs in England after GP funding withdrawn
items.summary:
Inquiry finds most integrated care boards have scrapped payments to GPs for prescribing and monitoring the drug

Patients who are eligible for potentially life-changing weight-loss injections on the NHS risk missing out after most integrated care boards (ICBs) in England withdrew funding for GP services, an investigation has found.

The inquiry, conducted by the GP magazine Pulse, found that 21 of 36 ICBs have scrapped payments to practices for prescribing and monitoring Mounjaro, also known as tirzepatide. A further nine never had a local enhanced service and only four still retain one.

Continue reading...
items.t: Patients may miss out on NHS weight-loss jabs in England after GP funding withdrawn

items.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
items.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.
items.t: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

items.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
items.summary: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.
items.t: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds

items.title: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts
items.summary:
Exclusive: Thirty-one trusts issue stark warning that cost-cutting demands threaten their ability to function normally

Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

Thirty-one health service trusts in England have issued stark warnings that NHS demands for them to make huge budget savings this year threaten their ability to function normally. All have declared that as a threat in the register of risks they have to maintain and publish.

Continue reading...
items.t: NHS savings drive leaves hospitals in England facing ‘unpalatable’ cuts

items.summary: The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer's, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.
items.t: Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back

items.title: French activists demand a tear gas suspension over reported menstrual changes
items.summary: Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints.
items.t: French activists demand a tear gas suspension over reported menstrual changes

items.title: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
items.summary:
From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex, a new book of short stories written by kids who are part of the "Read Alex" literacy program in Johannesburg. Participants in weekly classes wrote stories drawing on their own lives.'/> South Africa is working to overcome a children's literacy crisis. In one Johannesburg township, a reading club is instilling a love of books in kids — and inspiring them to become authors.

(Image credit: Madalene Cronje for NPR)
items.t: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa

items.title: An album to keep your mind on track | Brief letters
items.summary:
Steely Dan | Hot toddy | Dental advice | Christmas gifts | Black Friday

I read with interest how Adrian Chiles traces his concentration challenges back to the CD shuffle button (Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button, 18 November). The simple solution is to play Aja by Steely Dan, in its glorious 39 minutes and 54 seconds’ entirety, and I promise you there will be absolutely no skipping or shuffling of tracks.
Bren Pointer
London

• To mitigate the dental hygienist’s horror of a hot toddy (Letters, 20 November), how about having the hot water flavoured with sugar and lemon, followed by a swishing of the teeth with a generous helping of whisky?
William Bryce
Farnham, Surrey

Continue reading...
items.t: An album to keep your mind on track | Brief letters

items.title: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’
items.summary:
Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Continue reading...
items.t: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’

items.title: Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
items.summary:
Open enrollment for Medicare runs through Dec. 7, and there are a few different pitfalls people should watch out for this year. Your drug plan or Medicare Advantage plan could be changing a lot.

(Image credit: Joe Cavaretta/South Florida Sun Sentinel)
items.t: It's Medicare open enrollment time. Here's what you need to know

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
items.t: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.
items.t: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

items.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
items.t: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

items.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
items.summary: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.
items.t: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

items.title: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a common blood pressure drug can activate calorie-burning brown fat in mice, potentially opening a new path toward improving metabolic health. An analysis of more than 100,000 patients also revealed surprising links between brown fat and lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, anxiety, and depression.
items.t: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat

items.title: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
items.summary:
The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma – a blood cancer linked to the herbicide.

(Image credit: Justin Sullivan)
items.t: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions

items.title: A doctor's guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication
items.summary: Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.
items.t: A doctor's guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication

items.title: Cigarettes on silver platters at Bondi ‘clean’ beauty business lip gloss launch referred for investigation
items.summary:
Copini Beauty referred to New South Wales health regulators, while federal government says it is ‘deeply concerned’

Photos from an event held earlier in November at a venue in Bondi show what appears to be loose cigarettes without health warnings on a tiered silver platter alongside a bowl of lip glosses.

items.summary:
Death adds to national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 ⁠on Friday, involving a child who tested positive for the infectious disease, the state’s health department said.

The department said the child was ⁠age four or younger. It did not disclose additional details, including the child’s vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.

Continue reading...
items.t: Virginia child dies in state’s first measles-associated death of 2026

items.title: Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal
items.summary:
Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

Continue reading...
items.t: Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal

items.title: Philadelphia neonatologist Joanna Parga-Belinkie on keeping babies safe from measles
items.summary: Amid ongoing measles outbreaks, Philadelphia neonatologist Joanna Parga-Belinkie talks with NPR's Scott Simon about how she keeps infants too young for the vaccine safe.
items.t: Philadelphia neonatologist Joanna Parga-Belinkie on keeping babies safe from measles

items.title: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears
items.summary:
Experts say BBLs and other cosmetic procedures can be risky and seasonal offers at clinics in England could make people rush decisions

Clinics in England are promoting seasonal deals – including for Black Friday – on liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), despite concerns about the risks of the procedure.

The government is consulting on limiting liquid BBLs, vampire facials and deep chemical peels in England to qualified healthcare professionals. The proposals follow the death of Alice Webb, a 33-year-old mother of five, after a botched liquid BBL in a Gloucester salon in 2024. Her family have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people die.

Continue reading...
items.t: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears

items.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
items.summary: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.
items.t: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

items.title: It’s time we all made healthy food go further | Letters
items.summary:
Estelle Herszenhorn says the food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, while Lily van den Broecke and Charlie Wartnaby share tea ideas

Rachel Dixon’s article (The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November) shows how we can make healthy food go further, and the opportunity is bigger than many of us realise. The food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, and much of it is good fruit and vegetables that could have been eaten.

It’s not just peel and stalks we bin. WRAP found that date labels on fresh produce got in the way of people’s judgment, so more people said they would throw it out. Retailers have since removed those labels at scale, making it easier for all of us to use more of what we buy by default, and WRAP estimates that could save 50,000 tonnes a year.

Continue reading...
items.t: It’s time we all made healthy food go further | Letters

items.title: The best way to avoid winter illness | Letters
items.summary:
Responding to an article in the series The experts, Sally Billenness advocates wearing a mask and ensuring good ventilation. Plus, a letter by Caroline Clitter

“Stay hydrated”, “keep moisturised”, “go for a walk”, “be social”: while these are definitely good things for us to do, they are hardly the top of the list for avoiding winter ailments (Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments, 18 November). I am glad you have included vaccinations, but the two most useful things you can do don’t get a mention: wear a mask and ensure ventilation.

It’s flu season and airborne viruses such as Covid are still harming people, although as it is hardly ever reported you would not know it. People are being told that “it’s fine”, but as a long-Covid sufferer for 2.5 years, I can tell you this disease is vile: I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemy, certainly not my loved ones. I am unable to go for a walk, be social or stay active. If people feel ill (even “just a cold”) they should stay at home and avoid spreading their germs to everyone they meet, because they probably won’t know who is vulnerable.
Sally Billenness
Hounslow, London

Continue reading...
items.t: The best way to avoid winter illness | Letters

items.title: Bring in ‘cosmetic cowboys’ law to avoid more deaths, says family of butt lift victim
items.summary:
Relatives speak out as inquest jury finds Alice Webb’s death after filler entered her organs was accidental

The family of a woman who died after a botched Brazilian butt lift have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people lose their lives.

Speaking as an inquest jury concluded Alice Webb’s death was accidental, her family said they were astonished people were still having BBLs despite what had happened to her.

Continue reading...
items.t: Bring in ‘cosmetic cowboys’ law to avoid more deaths, says family of butt lift victim

items.title: ‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again
items.summary:
The US, Mexico and Bolivia this week joined the unenviable club of nations that have lost their measles-free status

Deaths caused by measles are not peaceful. In his hospital in Uganda, Dr Eric Wobudeya treats young infants after the virus has attacked their lungs and airways, or triggered pneumonia.

“These are children who are dying, and they are struggling for oxygen,” he said.

Continue reading...
items.t: As measles surges in countries where it was under control, children are paying the price

items.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
items.summary: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.
items.t: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

items.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
items.summary: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.
items.t: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's

items.title: Measles is officially back in the USA. Will Maha pay the price? - video
items.summary:
This week the US lost its measles elimination status, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the country after being eliminated for 26 years. To find out what this means in practical terms for citizens, Ian Sample hears from the Guardian US health reporter Jessica Glenza. She explains why it comes at an already difficult time for the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and his Make America Healthy Again movement, and what newly elected Democrats will be focusing on when it comes to health

Continue reading...
items.t: Measles is officially back in the USA. Will MAHA pay the price? - video

items.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’
items.summary:
Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing

A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.

In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

Continue reading...
items.t: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’

items.title: For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard
items.summary: A study of more than 10,000 college students found that exercising regularly may be more important for mental health than pushing yourself through intense or lengthy workouts. Students who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety a year later, suggesting that consistency could be a key ingredient in protecting mental well-being.
items.t: For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

items.title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat
items.summary:
Sadler’s Wells, London
In Six Lethargies, Iván Pérez and Seirian Griffiths have devised a mammoth production of aching, ethereal sadness

‘If I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz. If they dance it, will we feel it?

Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer Seirian Griffiths.

Continue reading...
items.t: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat

items.title: Patient ‘horrified’ to find her sensitive discussions were shared on system used by more than 100,000 NHS staff
items.summary:
Exclusive: Investigation launched after details of grief and trauma uploaded, raising questions over extent of issue

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation after a patient was “horrified” to discover that notes of sensitive discussions with her psychotherapist had been shared through a system used by more than 100,000 NHS workers.

Rosanna (not her real name) found out that her detailed therapist’s notes, including about her grief and trauma, had been uploaded to her patient records when she saw them on a computer screen during a visit to her GP.

Continue reading...
items.t: Patient ‘horrified’ to find her sensitive discussions were shared with more than 100,000 NHS staff

items.title: Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half
items.summary: A powerful experimental weight-loss drug helped people with knee osteoarthritis lose about 25% of their body weight at the highest dose, while roughly two-thirds experienced at least a 50% reduction in knee pain. The findings suggest retatrutide could transform treatment for millions suffering from painful arthritis, although its ability to prevent further joint damage remains unknown.
items.t: Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

items.title: A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best
items.summary: A major review involving more than 30,000 people found that three antidepressants, including Lexapro and Cymbalta, may be more effective than Prozac at maintaining improvements in depression symptoms. However, limitations in the research and a lack of truly long-term data mean scientists still cannot say which antidepressant is best.
items.t: A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
items.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.
items.t: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

items.title: Do you need a measles booster shot now that the U.S. has lost its elimination status?
items.summary: The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress.
items.t: Do you need a measles booster shot now that the U.S. has lost its elimination status?

items.title: For some patients, psychedelic treatment brings new troubles in its aftermath
items.summary: Psychedelics could transform mental health care, but some advocates and researchers say there needs to be more focus on the minority of people with persistent troubles after using these drugs.
items.t: For some patients, psychedelic treatment brings new troubles in its aftermath

items.title: Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
items.summary: Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.
items.t: Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals

items.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
items.summary:
How do we maintain healthy romantic relationships as we age? Allison Aubrey and Scott Detrow talk about about the science of healthy, later-in-life relationships.

(Image credit: Richard Drury/Getty Images)
items.t: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife

items.title: Call for police to investigate Scottish hospital after 19 deaths due to surgery
items.summary:
Surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary says he repeatedly voiced concerns and that patients may have died unnecessarily

A senior surgeon has called for a criminal investigation into a Scottish hospital after it emerged that at least 19 patients had died from avoidable complications due to surgery.

Dr Mohammed Habib, a consultant at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, said he had repeatedly reported concerns about the hospital’s liver and pancreatic surgery from 2021 onwards and believed dozens of patients may have died unnecessarily there.

Continue reading...
items.t: Call for police to investigate Scottish hospital after 19 deaths due to surgery

items.title: How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy
items.summary:
Experts agree that if you’re thinking of changing your diet, start small and keep your goals in mind

At this point, the environmental effects of the meat industry have been well-established: one 2021 study found that meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, and a 2025 report estimated that animal agriculture was responsible for 12%-19% of total human-caused greenhouse gases.

According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. Many of us know this, but in the US and UK, fewer than 5% of adults identify as vegetarian or vegan. One of the biggest obstacles, according to experts? People think it’s too hard.

Continue reading...
items.t: How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy

items.title: Trump takes 500 actions to weaken cancer protections, new report says
items.summary:
Natural Resources Defense Council shows how federal rules changes will increase public’s exposure to carcinogens

Amid a rise in early onset cancer, the Trump administration has taken more than 500 actions to systematically dismantle protections against carcinogens once in place across the federal government, an October report alleges.

The Natural Resources Defense Council report, and comments from current and former officials from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), brings into focus how myriad changes in federal rules or protocol will dramatically increase the public’s exposure to carcinogens. These are taking effect at a time when some forms of early onset cancer are spiking by about 30% per decade.

Continue reading...
items.t: Trump takes 500 actions to weaken cancer protections, new report says

items.title: World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
items.summary:
Yahoo for the loo! November 19 marks the 25th anniversary of World Toilet Day. The theme this year: "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." 

(Image credit: John Poole/Ryan Kellman/NPR )
items.t: Yahoo for the loo! An ode to the commode! Dotty for the potty! It's World Toilet Day!

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.
items.t: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

items.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
items.summary: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.
items.t: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.
items.t: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer

items.title: AP report: Bernie Sanders unveils how he'll push for Medicare for All when Democrats take power
items.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation's healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities.
items.t: AP report: Bernie Sanders unveils how he'll push for Medicare for All when Democrats take power

items.title: These women are Nepal's unsung heroes: shattered by the floods yet helping survivors
items.summary:
The floods of August took many lives, destroyed homes, hospitals and schools. Aid workers are taking up the hard work of rebuilding communities that suffered — even though they, too, saw great losses.

(Image credit: Family photos)
items.t: After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives

items.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
items.summary: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.
items.t: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

items.title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
items.summary:
In a statement celebrating the historic drop in drug deaths, the White House pointed to successes since President Trump took office. In fact, the biggest progress happened under the Biden administration.

(Image credit: Evan Vucci)
items.t: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit

items.title: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
items.summary: After dismantling the United States Agency for International Development, the Trump administration is restarting foreign aid. In Zambia and Zimbabwe, there are different approaches but similar worries.
items.t: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe

items.title: A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a rare, potentially life-threatening inflammatory disorder is driven by malfunctioning immune cells, overturning three decades of scientific understanding. The breakthrough points to a promising new treatment using existing medications, with one severely affected infant already showing substantial improvement.
items.t: A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

items.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
items.summary: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.
items.t: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

items.title: Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment
items.summary: Scientists have developed a new technique that uses magnetic nanoparticles to stimulate deep brain regions, dramatically improving Parkinson’s-like movement problems in mice without permanently implanted electrodes. The breakthrough could pave the way for less invasive treatments using injectable particles and wearable magnetic headbands.
items.t: Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

items.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
items.summary: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.
items.t: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
